blocks.title: Definitions
blocks.content:
Unless otherwise specified, the terms defined here apply as used in this document. They may have 
different meanings in other contexts.
Active (tuberculosis) case-finding: Provider-initiated screening and testing in communities by 
mobile teams, often using mobile X-ray and rapid molecular tests. The term is sometimes used 
synonymously with “systematic screening”.
Adherence: Extent to which a person’s behaviour (e.g. taking medicines, following a particular diet, 
changing lifestyle) corresponds with agreed recommendations from a health care provider.
Advanced HIV disease: For adolescents and

summary.text: Defines terms used in the guidelines, such as active case-finding, adherence, advanced HIV disease, adverse events and age groups from infant to adolescent. Many further definitions cover diagnostic, treatment, drug-resistance and outcome terms. Definitions apply to this document and may differ elsewhere. The section ends with references, including WHO consultations on outcome definitions.

blocks.title: Executive summary
blocks.content:
Introduction 
Children and young adolescents (aged below 15 years) represent about 11% of all people with 
tuberculosis (TB) globally. This means that 1.1 million children become ill with TB every year, almost 
half of them below five years of age. National TB programmes (NTPs) only notify less than half of 
these children, meaning that there is a large case detection gap (1). The reasons for this gap include 
challenges with specimen collection and bacteriological confirmation of TB in young children, due 
to the paucibacillary nature of TB disease in this age group and the lack of highly sen

summary.text: Summarises the 2022 guidelines, noting that about 1.1 million children fall ill with tuberculosis each year and fewer than half are notified, with low uptake of preventive treatment among young contacts. It sets out global targets, the rationale for updating the 2014 guidance, the objectives and the target audience. It lists the eight new recommendations, including Xpert Ultra as the first test on several specimen types, treatment decision algorithms, a 4-month regimen for non-severe tuberculosis, bedaquiline and delamanid for young children with drug-resistant tuberculosis and a 6-month regimen for tuberculous meningitis. A table of consolidated existing recommendations follows, covering areas such as HIV care, nutrition and contact investigation.

blocks.title: Background
blocks.content:
Children and young adolescents (aged below 15 years) represent about 11% of all people with TB 
globally. This means that close to 1.1 million children become ill with TB every year, almost half of them 
below five years of age. National TB programmes (NTPs) only notify less than half of these children, 
meaning that there is a large case detection gap (1). The reasons for this gap include challenges with 
specimen collection and bacteriological confirmation of TB in young children, due to the paucibacillary 
nature of TB disease in this age group and the lack of highly sensitive point-of-care

summary.text: Gives the background to the guidelines, noting the burden of tuberculosis in children and young adolescents, the case detection gap due to diagnostic difficulties and the 24% fall in child notifications in 2020 linked to COVID-19. It also mentions low preventive treatment coverage and explains that this update brings all relevant recommendations together in one guideline.

blocks.title: Rationale for the development of the 2022 consolidated guidelines
blocks.content:
consolidated guidelines 
Since the publication of the WHO Guidance for national tuberculosis programmes on the 
management of tuberculosis in children (second edition) (2014) (8), there have been numerous studies, 
including reviews, randomized controlled trials, observational studies, pharmacokinetic (PK) and 
pharmacodynamic studies, qualitative research and cost-effectiveness research, which have evaluated 
the impact of various interventions. These are related to diagnostic approaches for TB, treatment for 
drug-susceptible TB (DS-TB), drug-resistant TB (DR-TB) and TB meningitis (TBM), as

summary.text: Explains that new research since the 2014 WHO guidance on childhood tuberculosis prompted a review and update, with new and existing recommendations brought together in one consolidated guideline.

blocks.title: Objectives of the 2022 consolidated guidelines
blocks.content:
The objectives of the 2022 consolidated guidelines on the management of TB in children and 
adolescents are to:
1.	 provide policy-makers and implementing partners with evidence-based recommendations on the 
entire cascade of care for children and adolescents to support the implementation of activities 
to prevent TB among children and adolescents at risk, and to improve TB case detection and 
treatment outcomes in children and adolescents with TB, using effective models of care; and 
2.	 contribute to reductions in TB-related morbidity and mortality in children and adolescents in 
line with g

summary.text: States the guidelines' objectives: to give evidence-based recommendations across the cascade of care for children and adolescents and to help cut tuberculosis illness and death in line with global targets.

blocks.title: Target audience
blocks.content:
The target audience for these consolidated guidelines consists primarily of NTPs, primary health 
care (PHC) programmes, maternal and child health programmes, national AIDS programmes (or 
their equivalents in health ministries) and other health policy-makers. They also target generalist 
and specialist paediatricians, clinicians and health practitioners working on TB, HIV and/or infectious 
diseases in public and private sectors, the educational sector, nongovernmental, civil society and 
community-based organizations, as well as technical and implementing partners.

summary.text: Identifies the target audience as tuberculosis, primary care, maternal and child health and AIDS programmes, clinicians, and civil society and implementing partners.

blocks.title: WHO recommendations relevant to the management of TB in children and adolescents
blocks.content:
management of TB in children and adolescents
The 2022 consolidated guidelines represent a significant update compared to the previous guidelines 
issued in 2014. They include: (i) new recommendations based on the review of newly available 
evidence related to the Population, Intervention, Comparator and Outcomes (PICO) questions that 
were developed for this guideline update; (ii) recommendations with relevance to children and 
adolescents from other WHO TB guidelines issued since 2014; and (iii) a few recommendations from 
the 2014 guidance that remain unchanged. These latter recommendations

summary.text: Explains that the 2022 WHO consolidated guidelines on managing TB in children and adolescents combine new evidence-based recommendations, relevant recommendations from other WHO TB guidelines since 2014 and some unchanged 2014 recommendations. It notes that source wording and age definitions are kept and points users to the WHO TB Knowledge Sharing Platform and web annexes.

blocks.title: Scope of the guideline update
blocks.content:
The population of interest in these guidelines is children and adolescents, defined as:
•	 A child is a person under 10 years of age.
•	 An adolescent is a person 10–19 years of age (inclusive).
The pathway of TB infection and disease in an individual child or adolescent, and the interface with 
and retention across sequential stages of care (termed the ‘cascade of care’) was used as the analytic 
framework during the scoping process for this guideline update (Figure 1) (10). This pathway involves 
multiple steps from exposure to a person with an infectious form of TB, leading to subsequent TB

summary.text: Sets the scope of the guideline update, defining children as under 10 and adolescents as 10–19 years, and uses the cascade of care from TB exposure to treatment outcome as its analytical framework, shown in a figure. It lists the PICO questions addressed, on diagnosis, treatment and models of care such as decentralized and family-centred integrated services. Two background questions concern the socioeconomic impact of TB on families and how best to engage adolescents in care.

blocks.title: Publication, dissemination, evaluation and expiry
blocks.content:
The electronic version of the consolidated guidelines on the management of TB in children and 
adolescents will form part of the WHO TB KSP, which features the following components for each TB 
module: (i) consolidated guidelines, (ii) operational handbooks with implementation guidance; as well 
as (iii) a catalogue of WHO e-learning materials.
Further dissemination strategies include global, regional and country webinars and consultations, 
development of training materials based on the guideline and the operational handbook, and technical 
support for countries during programme reviews and o

summary.text: Describes how the guidelines will be published on the WHO TB Knowledge Sharing Platform and disseminated through webinars, training and technical support, and lists the age-disaggregated indicators that will be monitored. It states that the recommendations will be reviewed within five years, and the interim recommendation on treatment decision algorithms within two years.

summary.text: Outlines the structure of the 2022 guidelines chapter by chapter, from the introduction through screening and contact investigation, prevention, diagnosis and treatment to care of children with TB and HIV or malnutrition. It notes which chapters contain new recommendations and that the final chapter sets out research priorities.

blocks.title: TB screening and contact investigation
blocks.content:
2. TB screening and contact 
investigation
This chapter includes current WHO recommendations that apply to children and adolescents on TB 
screening and contact investigation. They have been consolidated from current WHO guidelines 
on systematic screening for TB disease and contact investigation, namely the WHO consolidated 
guidelines on tuberculosis. Module 2: screening – systematic screening for tuberculosis disease (11) 
and Guidance for national tuberculosis programmes on the management of tuberculosis in children 
(second edition) (8). For more information on each recommendation includi

summary.text: Opens chapter 2 by consolidating existing WHO recommendations on TB screening and contact investigation relevant to children and adolescents. Table 3 lists recommendations such as systematically screening household contacts and people living with HIV, and HIV counselling and testing of contacts depending on HIV prevalence.

blocks.title: Prevention of TB
blocks.content:
This chapter includes current WHO recommendations that apply to children and adolescents on TB 
prevention. They have been consolidated from current WHO guidelines on TB infection, prevention 
and control, a BCG position paper and guidelines on TPT, namely the WHO guidelines on tuberculosis 
infection prevention and control, 2019 update (12), the BCG vaccines: WHO position paper (published in 
the Weekly Epidemiological Record) (13) and the WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis. Module 1: 
prevention – tuberculosis preventive treatment (14). For more information on each recommendation 
i

summary.text: Consolidates WHO recommendations on TB prevention relevant to children and adolescents, drawn from guidelines on infection prevention and control, the BCG vaccine position paper and guidelines on TB preventive treatment. Table 4 lists measures such as triage and respiratory isolation of people with TB symptoms, BCG vaccination, testing for TB infection and preventive treatment regimens. Recommendations on preventive therapy for people living with HIV, including 36 months of isoniazid in high-transmission settings, close the section.

blocks.title: Diagnostic approaches for TB in children and adolescents
blocks.content:
in children and adolescents
Of the estimated 1.1 million children who developed TB annually, only 399 000 (36.5%) were notified 
to NTPs in 2020. Under-notification is worst among children below 5 years of age, with only 27.5% of 
children with TB being notified (1). These ‘missing’ children are not diagnosed and/or not reported. 
TB-related mortality among children below 15 years of age was estimated at 226 000 for 2020 (1). 
Modelling has shown that 80% of TB-related deaths are among children under 5 years of age, and 
that 96% of children who die of TB, did not access treatment (15).
The lo

summary.text: Describes the gap in TB diagnosis among children, with only about a third of an estimated 1.1 million cases notified in 2020 and most deaths occurring in under-fives who never received treatment. It explains causes such as paucibacillary disease, lack of a sensitive point-of-care test, sampling difficulties and limited primary care capacity, and notes a 2021 expert consultation advising that intrathoracic lymph node TB be classified as pulmonary TB.

blocks.title: The use of the Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra assay in gastric aspirate and stool specimens for the diagnosis of pulmonary TB and rifampicin resistance
blocks.content:
in gastric aspirate and stool specimens for the 
diagnosis of pulmonary TB and rifampicin resistance
Recommendation:
In children with signs and symptoms of pulmonary TB, Xpert Ultra should be used as the 
initial diagnostic test for TB and detection of rifampicin resistance on sputum, nasopharyngeal 
aspirate, gastric aspirate or stool, rather than smear microscopy/culture and phenotypic drug 
susceptibility testing (DST). 
(Strong recommendation, moderate certainty of evidence for test accuracy in stool and gastric 
aspirate; low certainty of evidence for test accuracy in sputum; very low cer

summary.text: Recommends Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra as the initial test for pulmonary TB and rifampicin resistance in children using sputum, nasopharyngeal aspirate, gastric aspirate or stool, instead of smear microscopy, culture and phenotypic drug susceptibility testing. It sets out the justification and evidence, noting the limited sensitivity of the earlier Xpert MTB/RIF assay among children and people with HIV. Implementation considerations cover acceptability and feasibility of specimen collection, and monitoring advice covers laboratory registers and reporting notifications by five-year age group.

In children with presumptive pulmonary TB attending health care facilities, integrated treatment 
decision algorithms may be used to diagnose pulmonary TB. 
(Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence).
Remarks
•	Presumptive TB refers to a person who presents with symptoms and/or signs suggestive of 
TB.24
•	Bacteriological confirmation should be sought as part of the integrated treatment decision 
algorithms whenever possible, using WHO recommended rapid diagnostic tests and 
appropriate paediatric

summary.text: Gives an interim conditional recommendation that integrated treatment decision algorithms may be used to diagnose pulmonary TB in children under 10 with presumptive TB, while still seeking bacteriological confirmation where possible. It explains that new algorithms are detailed in the operational handbook and that the recommendation will be reviewed after 24 months. The section covers the evidence, the need to suspect drug-resistant TB where relevant, and monitoring of treatment response and outcomes.

blocks.title: Treatment of TB disease in children and adolescents
blocks.content:
WHO recommendations that apply to the treatment of TB in children and adolescents (section 5.4). 
The four new recommendations concern drug-susceptible TB (DS-TB): (i) a four-month regimen for 
children and adolescents below 16 years of age with non-severe drug-susceptible TB (section 5.1); 
(ii) a six-month intensive regimen to treat TBM composed of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and 
ethionamide (section 5.2); (iii) use of bedaquiline as part of shorter or longer regimens for children 
of all ages to treat MDR/RR-TB (section 5.3.1); and (iv) use of delamanid as part of longer regimens

summary.text: Introduces the treatment chapter, listing four new recommendations: a four-month regimen for non-severe drug-susceptible TB, a six-month intensive regimen for TB meningitis, and bedaquiline and delamanid for children of all ages with MDR/RR-TB. It notes the source guidelines from which other treatment recommendations are consolidated.

blocks.title: Treatment shortening in children and adolescents with non-severe TB
blocks.content:
adolescents with non-severe TB
Recommendation:
In children and adolescents between 3 months and 16 years of age with non-severe TB (without 
suspicion or evidence of MDR/RR-TB), a 4-month treatment regimen (2HRZ(E)/2HR) should 
be used.
(Strong recommendation, moderate certainty of evidence)
Remarks
•	Non-severe TB is defined as: Peripheral lymph node TB; intrathoracic lymph node TB without 
airway obstruction; uncomplicated TB pleural effusion or paucibacillary, non-cavitary disease, 
confined to one lobe of the lungs, and without a miliary pattern.
•	Children and adolescents who do not meet

summary.text: Recommends a four-month regimen for children and adolescents aged 3 months to 16 years with non-severe TB, defining non-severe disease and advising the standard six-month regimen for others. It notes ethambutol should be added in settings with high HIV or isoniazid resistance prevalence. The justification cites potential benefits of shorter treatment for costs, toxicity, drug interactions and adherence. Implementation considerations stress accurate classification of severity and follow-up for up to 12 months after treatment to detect relapse.

blocks.title: Treatment regimens for TB meningitis in children and adolescents
blocks.content:
and adolescents
Recommendation
In children and adolescents with bacteriologically confirmed or clinically diagnosed TB meningitis 
(without suspicion or evidence of MDR/RR-TB), a 6-month intensive regimen (6HRZEto) may be 
used as an alternative option to the 12-month regimen (2HRZE/10HR) 
(Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of the evidence).
Remarks
•	The shorter intensive regimen is suitable for children and adolescents who have no evidence of 
drug resistance and in children and adolescents who have a low likelihood of drug-resistant TB, 
e.g. those without risk factors for any

summary.text: Gives a conditional recommendation that a six-month intensive regimen of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethionamide may be used as an alternative to the 12-month regimen for TB meningitis in children and adolescents without drug resistance. It notes the 12-month regimen remains an option and that the shorter regimen should not be used in those living with HIV owing to lack of data. Evidence, diagnostic considerations and monitoring of uptake and outcomes are also covered.

blocks.title: Treatment of multi-drug and rifampicin resistant TB in children
blocks.content:
TB in children 
Around 25 000–32 000 children are estimated to develop MDR/RR-TB every year (75–77). In 2018, 
3398 children (aged below 15 years) were started on second-line treatment for MDR/RR-TB. After 
increasing to 5586 in 2019, due to the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, this number dropped back 
to 3234 in 2020, representing only 2.5% of the total number of persons with MDR/RR-TB initiated on 
treatment and only 10.1%–12.9% of the estimated number of children with incident MDR/RR-TB (78). 
Treatment outcomes reported in a systematic review and individual patient data meta-analysis 
con

summary.text: Addresses treatment of MDR/RR-TB in children, noting an estimated 25 000–32 000 cases a year but only a few thousand started on second-line treatment, with numbers falling during COVID-19. It presents the recommendation on bedaquiline for children of all ages, explaining that earlier advice applied only from age 6 because of limited pharmacokinetic and safety data in younger children. It then covers delamanid for children of all ages within longer regimens. Implementation and monitoring points include the risk of delamanid resistance, cardiac and neuropsychiatric safety monitoring, and recording treatment outcomes.

blocks.title: Models of TB care for case detection and provision of TPT in children and adolescents
blocks.content:
detection and provision of TPT 
in children and adolescents
This chapter contains two new recommendations and other valid WHO recommendations that 
apply to patient support and models of care (section 6.2). The two new recommendations, on the 
implementation of decentralized models of care and integrated family-centred models of care to 
improve both case detection and the provision of TPT, are described in full detail as this information 
is being published for the first time. Other consolidated recommendations in this chapter are related 
to patient support, health education and counselling,

summary.text: Introduces the chapter on models of TB care for case detection and preventive treatment in children and adolescents, noting two new recommendations and other consolidated ones on patient support. It describes how paediatric TB capacity is often centralised, primary care staff lack confidence and many chances for contact tracing and prevention are missed, which frames the questions on decentralised and family-centred care.

blocks.title: Decentralized and family-centred, integrated models of care to deliver child and adolescent TB services
blocks.content:
models of care to deliver child and adolescent TB 
services 
Recommendations:
In TB high burden settings, decentralized models of care may be used to deliver TB services 
to children and adolescents with signs and symptoms of TB and/or those exposed to TB 
(conditional recommendation, very low certainty evidence).
Family-centred, integrated models of care to deliver TB services may be used in children 
and adolescents with signs and symptoms of TB and/or those exposed to TB, in addition to 
standard models of care (conditional recommendation, very low certainty evidence).
Remarks
•	These recom

summary.text: Sets out two new conditional recommendations, based on very low certainty evidence, that decentralised and family-centred, integrated models of care are options for delivering TB services to children and adolescents with TB symptoms or exposure. Remarks clarify that decentralisation strengthens services at lower levels rather than replacing specialist care, and should target areas with poor access or high prevalence. The section then presents the justification and evidence and implementation considerations, including differentiated service delivery. It ends with monitoring and evaluation advice on planning, registers, sex-disaggregated data and service quality.

blocks.title: Special situations
blocks.content:
7. Special situations 
This chapter includes valid WHO recommendations that apply to children and adolescents in 
special situations such as for the management of TB in the context of HIV infection or malnutrition 
and optimal feeding of infants of mothers infected with TB. The recommendations have been 
consolidated from several current WHO guidelines on TB/HIV coinfection and nutrition, namely 
the WHO policy on collaborative TB/HIV activities: guidelines for national programmes and other 
stakeholders (124), the Consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, testing, treatment, service delivery

summary.text: Opens the chapter on special situations, covering WHO recommendations for TB in children and adolescents with HIV or malnutrition and feeding of infants of mothers with TB. Table 8 gathers recommendations on HIV testing, co-trimoxazole prophylaxis, antiretroviral therapy eligibility and timing, and TB/HIV care. It also includes nutritional recommendations, such as managing severe acute malnutrition, and ends with a note on pyridoxine with isoniazid.

blocks.title: Research priorities
blocks.content:
8. Research priorities
This chapter includes research gaps or priorities that were identified by the GDG members while 
considering the evidence related to each of the PICO questions. Addressing the identified research 
gaps has the potential to inform the development of future research questions that can improve 
TB prevention and care. This list of research priorities is not exhaustive; but it complements the 
existing research agenda outlined in Research priorities for paediatric tuberculosis (127) and other 
WHO guidelines. 
TB screening (adapted from WHO consolidated guidelines on tubercu

summary.text: Lists research gaps identified by the guideline development group, grouped by topic such as TB screening, diagnostic approaches and treatment decision algorithms. The priorities call for studies on screening tools for different age groups, validation and implementation of diagnostic algorithms, and research on community perceptions and the quality of TB diagnosis in children.

summary.text: A long annex table comparing each recommendation in WHO's 2014 guidance on managing TB in children with its current status in this module. For each item it gives the original wording and source, whether it was updated, kept, copied to the operational handbook or replaced, and the new wording.
